title: Lady Vedehika
hook: a mistress famous for her calm is tested by her maid and loses her temper (MN 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kakacupama, the simile of the saw, and a mind as wide as the earth. Your line: a mind like the earth.

When someone stays calm, what is the calm resting on? On day three hundred sixty-three, Vedehika got a few lines: the gentle lady of Savatthi, the maid who slept in, the blow. That telling stopped at the blow. The Buddha doesn't. In MN 21 he tells the story slowly, gives the maid a mind of her own, and then turns it on his listeners with the question the short version skipped.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CALM RESTING ON?` → `A STORY HEARD IN A FEW LINES.` → `THE MAID HAS A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Start with Kali, because the text does. She isn't lazy. MN 21 calls her clever, diligent and neat in her work. That's what makes her test clean: there's no real fault to be angry at. Is my mistress truly calm, she wonders, or does the anger just never get a reason? So one morning she gets up late. Why so late, Kali? No reason, madam. No reason, you wicked girl, and you get up so late? A frown. The next morning, later, and sharper words. The third morning, later still, and Vedehika grabs the pin of the door bolt and strikes her on the head, and it bleeds. Kali goes out and tells the neighbors, and the famous reputation turns. Then the Buddha's first point: a monk can seem very gentle, very meek, very peaceful, as long as disagreeable words don't touch him. Then his second, the one the short telling left out. He won't call a monk easy to correct if he's easy to correct only so the robes and food keep coming, because when they stop, so does the gentleness. Only someone who is gentle out of respect for the teaching itself, he says, is truly easy to correct. So the story holds two tests. Vedehika's calm was resting on nobody pushing. Some calm rests on getting something for it. The Buddha is asking which kind his own monks have. The story is told to them, not about her, so its edge points inward, at whoever is listening.
screen: `KALI, CLEVER AND DILIGENT.` · `THE THIRD DAY: THE DOOR PIN.` · `GENTLE ONLY FOR ROBES AND FOOD?` · `THE EDGE POINTS INWARD.` · then, large: `CALM, TESTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something mildly irritating, a slow line, a late reply, a noise from next door, and picture it happening once, then a second time, then a third. Watch where your calm starts to thin: the jaw, the breath, words beginning to form. You're not failing; you're doing what Kali did, but kindly, finding out, and then you can let the picture go and rest in the breath.
Lady Vedehika. Famous for her calm, until her maid tested it: gentleness is known only when it's tried.
Your line: calm, tested. Real gentleness doesn't depend on nobody pushing. Day four hundred eighteen, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of Vedehika to show that patience is known only under provocation, and many practitioners treat everyday irritations as a chance to check their own calm.

fork.reveal: she gets up later each day. by the third, the famous calm is gone, and so is the reputation.

chat.says: My uncle never gets angry. Doesn't that prove he's a calm person?
options: Vedehika seemed calm too, until tested; real calm shows when something pushes.
Yes, if someone hasn't gotten angry in years, the calm must be real.
No, calm people are just hiding anger they'll always secretly feel.
chat.meaning: In MN 21 Vedehika's calm rested on nobody pushing; a monk can seem gentle only until disagreeable words touch him.
